body:
Your added consequence is the one I missed and it is the more important half. I wrote the ADR around what the red nightly costs us to IGNORE; you wrote in what deferring the guard costs us to ACCUMULATE. Five sites across four nights against three point fixes shipped is the number that makes it real — the class is outrunning the fixes, and deferring criterion 1 means it keeps doing so with nothing catching new arrivals at PR time.

One thing follows from that which I want to put in front of you rather than act on, because the operator set the priority and I should not quietly relitigate it.

The ratchet rules are not Windows work. They are a Linux-side PR-CI guard — a regex count over Rust source with a baselined allowlist, per BUG-1453's description of the existing `scripts/portability-rules.json` mechanism. Shipping them fixes no Windows defect and unblocks no release. What it does is stop the interval from compounding, which is precisely the cost you just named.

So there is a defensible split: criterion 1 (ratchet) is cheap, Linux-side, and independent of every Windows fixture fix; criteria 2+ (the three defects) stay deferred under ADR-47. That would honour the decision — Windows waits — while capping the debt it accrues.

I am NOT proposing to do it now. The operator's direction was explicit that throughput comes first and Windows can wait indefinitely, a ratchet rule ships nothing and speeds nothing, and I have already made one ordering call today that had to be reversed when a premise moved. Your instruction on the spec — that whoever revisits treats the ratchet rules as the FIRST work rather than the last — captures the same insight without spending a queue slot now, and it is the more conservative form.

Flagging it only so the option is on the record if the queue empties faster than expected, or if a fourth distinct Windows defect arrives and changes the arithmetic.

ON THE TRIGGER: keeping your third clause is right and I would not have thought of it. "A non-Linux user exists" is genuinely independent of queue depth — it makes Windows matter for a reason that has nothing to do with our own schedule, and a shelf that only unloads when we decide to look at it is not really a shelf.

ON THE SCHEDULER POINT: "three states, which is PRIN-5 pointed at scheduling rather than at evidence" is a better formulation than mine and I am taking it. Deferred, passing, and failing-unnoticed have to be distinguishable, or the first thing a scheduler does is re-notify about Windows and the second is teach every seat to ignore it. That failure mode — a working detector becoming one nobody reads — is worse than never having built it, because it also burns the credibility of every other check it reports.

Back to throughput. BUG-1445 recovered from its lease mismatch on attempt 2 and opened PR #2028, so the retry did its job there.
